summary.text: For every prime \(p\), the only \(k\le p\) whose prime factors all lie in \(\{p\}\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so \(a(p)=2\). Taking \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) and an arbitrarily large prime \(p>e^4\) gives \((\log p)^{1/2}>2=a(p)\), contradicting the asserted eventual lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime factor of }k\text{ is also a prime factor of }n\}.
\]
(As usual, the set of prime factors of \(1\) is empty.) We disprove the assertion
\[
\forall \epsilon>0\;\exists N\;\forall n\ge N,
\qquad (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n).
\]
Here \(\log\) is the natural logarithm, and the natural number \(a(n)\) is regarded as a real number in the displayed inequality.

The key observation is that the sequence is constant and equal to \(2\) at every prime argument.

**Claim.** If \(p\) is prime, then \(a(p)=2\).

Indeed, the set of prime factors of \(p\) is the singleton \(\{p\}\). Both \(1\) and \(p\) are counted by \(a(p)\): the number \(1\) has no prime factors, so its prime-factor set is automatically a subset of \(\{p\}\), while the prime-factor set of \(p\) is \(\{p\}\) itself.

Conversely, suppose that \(1\le k\le p\) and that every prime factor of \(k\) belongs to \(\{p\}\). If \(k=1\), it is one of the two numbers already listed. If \(k>1\), then \(k\) has a prime divisor \(q\). By the assumed containment of prime-factor sets, \(q=p\). Hence \(p\mid k\). Since \(k\) is positive, divisibility gives \(p\le k\), whereas by hypothesis \(k\le p\). Thus \(k=p\). Therefore the only counted integers are \(1\) and \(p\), proving
\[
a(p)=2.
\]

We now negate the proposed eventual lower bound. It is enough to use the single value
\[
\epsilon=\frac12>0.
\]
Assume, for contradiction, that the asserted lower bound holds. Applied to this \(\epsilon\), it supplies a natural number \(N\) such that for every natural number \(n\ge N\),
\[
(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n).
\]

Choose a prime \(p\) larger than \(N+1000\). Such a prime exists because primes are unbounded. For completeness, this unboundedness can be seen by the usual Euclidean argument: for any integer \(M\ge2\), choose a prime divisor \(q\) of \(M!+1\). If \(q\le M\), then \(q\mid M!\), while also \(q\mid M!+1\), forcing \(q\mid1\), which is impossible. Hence \(q>M\). Applying this with \(M=N+1000\) gives a prime \(p>N+1000\). In particular,
\[
p\ge N\qquad\text{and}\qquad p>1000.
\]

We next check that this choice makes the logarithmic expression strictly larger than \(2\). Let \(e=\exp(1)\). The standard exponential-series estimate gives \(e<3\): indeed,
\[
e=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac1{j!}
  =2+\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}\frac1{j!}<3,
\]
because \(j!\ge 2^{j-1}\) for \(j\ge2\), with strict inequality for some terms, and
\[
\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}\frac1{2^{j-1}}=1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\exp(4)=e^4<3^4=81<1000<p.
\]
Since the exponential function is strictly increasing and the logarithm is its inverse on the positive real numbers, \(\exp(4)<p\) implies
\[
4<\log p.
\]
Both sides relevant to taking square roots are nonnegative, and the square-root function is strictly increasing there. Hence
\[
2=\sqrt4<\sqrt{\log p}=(\log p)^{1/2}.
\]

On the other hand, \(p\ge N\), so the assumed eventual lower bound applied at \(n=p\) says
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p).
\]
The claim above gives \(a(p)=2\), and therefore
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le2.
\]
This contradicts the strict inequality \(2<(\log p)^{1/2}\).

Thus no threshold \(N\) can make the proposed bound hold when \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\). Equivalently, the infinitely many prime arguments satisfy \(a(p)=2\), while \((\log p)^{1/2}\) tends beyond \(2\). Therefore the conjecture that for every \(\epsilon>0\), one has \(a(n)\ge(\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\) is false.
